narrative:
The model estimates an 11% chance that you will fail your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this is the same as the average for students who passed, in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees it as unexpectedly low effort relative to your other choices, nudging the outcome toward failure. The second strongest influence is your weekly study time of 5–10 hours. Although this is higher than many students, it is still lower than the amount put in by most who ultimately pass, pulling the prediction slightly toward failing. Third, having your father as guardian also contributes a modest push in the failing direction, differing from the 69% of passing students who have their mother as guardian.

Taken together, these elements outweigh the many positive signals in your profile, such as wanting higher education, having internet access, strong family relationships, and zero absences.

To improve, you should aim to increase your consistent study time beyond 10 hours a week, seek extra academic support from teachers or tutors, and perhaps discuss with your father how he and your mother can jointly monitor your progress. Small, steady changes in these areas can meaningfully raise your chances of passing. (218 words)
